title: Lipoma
subject: Pathology
summary: A lipoma is a benign tumor of mature adipocytes, usually subcutaneous and slow‑growing. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by simple imaging; treatment is excision if symptomatic or for diagnosis.

sections.p: Lipoma is a well‑circumscribed, soft, mobile mass composed of mature fat cells. It is diagnosed by history and physical exam; ultrasound or fine‑needle aspiration (FNA) can confirm when needed.
b: Usually <5 cm, but giant lipomas >10 cm exist

sections.p: Lipomas are benign and not staged, but size, depth, and symptomatology guide management. Giant lipomas (>10 cm or >1 kg) may cause functional impairment.
b: Rapid growth or fixation – rule out liposarcoma

sections.p: Most lipomas are idiopathic. Risk factors include genetics (familial multiple lipomatosis), trauma, and obesity. In low‑resource settings, consider HIV‑associated lipodystrophy as a mimic.
Patients notice a painless, slowly enlarging lump, often on the trunk, neck, or extremities. Occasionally the mass may become painful if it compresses nerves or is traumatized.
b: May be multiple in familial cases

sections.p: Imaging and cytology help differentiate lipoma from malignant or infectious lesions, especially when the presentation is atypical.

t.b: Is the mass cystic or solid and what are its borders? – Shows a homogeneous, hyperechoic, well‑defined lesion consistent with fat.
What cells are present? – Yields mature adipocytes without atypia; helps rule out liposarcoma when cytology is uncertain.
Is there deep tissue involvement or suspicious features? – Lipoma appears hyperintense on T1, suppresses with fat‑sat; irregular septa or nodularity suggest liposarcoma.

sections.p: Although benign, certain features warrant urgent evaluation for malignancy or infection.
b: Pain, ulceration, or overlying skin change

sections.p: Treatment is conservative unless the lipoma is symptomatic, cosmetically concerning, or suspicious for malignancy.
b: Surgical excision under local anaesthesia for symptomatic or diagnostic purposes
Avoid liposuction in deep or large lesions where capsule integrity is needed

sections.p: Routine follow‑up is only needed after excision to monitor wound healing. No proven primary prevention; weight control may reduce new lesions in predisposed individuals.
b: Educate patient to report new rapid growth

sections.p: Several other soft‑tissue masses can mimic lipoma clinically.
b: Lipoma vs. well‑differentiated liposarcoma – requires imaging or genetic test (MDM2/CDK4 amplification)
Lipoma vs. epidermoid cyst – cystic centre, central punctum
Lipoma vs. lymphadenopathy – firmer, less mobile

sections.p: Imaging and cytology may be equivocal, especially in resource‑limited settings.
b: Ultrasound may miss deep infiltrative liposarcoma
FNA can sample only peripheral fat, missing focal atypia

whenToSeekHelp: Pain, ulceration, or overlying skin colour change
Systemic symptoms such as fever or weight loss

faq.a: A true lipoma does not turn malignant, but a rapidly growing, fixed mass may be a liposarcoma and needs evaluation.

faq.q: Is liposuction a safe way to remove a lipoma?
faq.a: Liposuction may leave residual tissue and makes pathological assessment difficult; excision is preferred when diagnosis is uncertain.
Recurrence is uncommon if the capsule is completely excised; incomplete removal can lead to regrowth.

exam: What bedside features distinguish a lipoma from an inflamed lymph node? — Soft, doughy consistency, mobility, lack of tenderness, and absence of systemic signs.
A 45‑year‑old farmer presents with a 12 cm painless thigh mass. What is your next investigative step and why? — Obtain ultrasound to confirm a homogeneous fatty lesion before planning excision.
How would you manage a subcutaneous mass that is mobile but has grown rapidly over 2 weeks? — Treat as possible liposarcoma: order MRI (or refer for imaging) and arrange biopsy before excision.
Why is fine‑needle aspiration sometimes insufficient to rule out liposarcoma? — It samples only superficial cells and may miss atypical deep components; imaging or core biopsy is needed.

In a low‑resource clinic without MRI, how can you differentiate a lipoma from a deep‑seated sarcoma? — Use high‑resolution ultrasound for internal septa, assess growth pattern, and refer for surgical excision with histology if suspicion persists.

What are the contraindications to surgical excision of a lipoma in a patient with uncontrolled HIV on antiretroviral therapy? — Poor wound healing risk, thrombocytopenia, and drug interactions; optimise HIV control before elective surgery.

Explain why a giant lipoma may cause functional impairment and how you would assess it. — Size can compress nerves or limit joint movement; assess range of motion, neurovascular status, and pain on movement.

A patient reports a ‘fatty lump’ that feels firm and fixed. What red‑flag condition must you exclude and what test confirms it? — Exclude well‑differentiated liposarcoma; MRI with fat‑suppression and, if available, MDM2/CDK4 amplification testing.
